1. On the day of the storm, on the day when heaven and earth were fashioned,  
2. In the night of the storm, in the night when heaven and earth were fashioned,  
3. In the year of the storm, the year when fate was decreed,  
4. The Anunnaki assembled and marched forth.  
5. Damadina bore the title of “Chief Exorcist.”  
6. Damadina traversed heaven and earth.  
7. Damadina […] gave birth, and she bore [a child].  
8. The god of the mountain, whose name is [lacuna], and whose “city” (?) is [lacuna], was established there.  
9. The lord of lords, the god of the foundation, commands the minor gods; they stand about him in awe.  
10. The god of the river, whose name is Dun-dun (and who is) “the one of the muddy banks,” made the soil tremble, and caused the earth to quake.  
11. The god of the wind, whose name is Ar-ar, uttered his pure word; his command was established.  
12. At that time, profound wisdom, abundant knowledge, and the god of the lordship—abundant—were manifest.  
13. Enki, lord of the subterranean waters, opened up the deep canals, the pure waters, the waters of the Abzu; the deity had no name, yet its heart was directed toward the heavenly vault.  
14. Its foundation did not yet stand firm, nor did its mound yet rise up.  
15. Er-ra, the god and his divine companions, stood forth in full strength; they spoke words of command.  
16. The man of the “red land” (Kurra) stood there—its foundation did not yet rise up.  
17. Namma gave birth to her mother Palil, and the lord of lords (šar2-šar2) was born.  
18. Er-ra, the divine ones, brought his son forward.  
19. [Name?] caused it to be settled; and caused them to be settled.  
20. [Name?] … was established; it did not yet rise up.  
21. Dimmer, whose hands are skillful, whose foundation (?) is [lacuna], whose weight (?) makes the earth tremble.  

Notes:  
- This passage appears to be a fragment of a Sumerian cosmogonic or mythological composition, possibly related to creation, divine assembly, or the emergence of cosmic order. The text contains numerous lacunae (indicated by brackets or X) and uncertain readings, common in heavily damaged cuneiform tablets.  
- Orthographic variants (e.g., “šar2-šar2” for “lord of lords”, “ĝi6” for “night”, “ud” for “day”) are normalized in translation.  
- Terms like “NIR.PA” (a high-ranking exorcist/priestly office), “Anunnaki”, “Abzu”, and “Er-ra” (a storm/war god) reflect well-attested Sumerian theological concepts.  
- Line 17’s mention of Namma (primeval mother goddess) giving birth to Palil—and that the “lord of lords” was born—suggests a generational theogony.  
- The repetitive structures (lines 1–3, 12, 14, 16, 20) reflect typical Sumerian literary parallelism and cosmic staging.  
- Translations of ambiguous or partially reconstructed signs (e.g., line 8 “unu2?”, line 21 “gu2?”) are marked with question marks or noted as uncertain.
